label: CSIR-UGC NET Methods of Estimation (2011–2025) — regression PYQs

items.topic: regression-t2 · relationship between the two simple-regression slopes
items.stem: For a bivariate data set, one analyst fits Y on X and another fits X on Y, both by ordinary least squares with an intercept. Which pair (slope of Y on X, slope of X on Y) is possible?
items.explanation: The two regression slopes are b(Y on X)=r·sY/sX and b(X on Y)=r·sX/sY. Multiplying them cancels the standard deviations and gives r². Therefore the slopes must have the same sign, and their product must lie between 0 and 1. Option D has two negative slopes and product (−2)(−0.4)=0.8, which is possible. The other options either have opposite signs or a product greater than 1. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation or regression is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: regression-t2 · OLS normal equations without an intercept
items.stem: Consider the multiple regression model Yᵢ=β₁Xᵢ₁+⋯+βₚXᵢₚ+εᵢ, with no intercept. Let êᵢ be the ordinary least-squares residual. Which statements are always true?
statements: Σᵢêᵢ=0 and ΣᵢXᵢⱼêᵢ=0 for every regressor j.

A.why: The model has no intercept, so the sum of residuals need not be zero.

B.why: The OLS normal equations make the residual vector orthogonal to every column of the design matrix.

C.why: It adds the unsupported claim that residuals must sum to zero.

D.why: Y′ê=ê′ê, which is generally positive unless all residuals are zero.

items.explanation: OLS chooses the coefficients to minimise the sum of squared residuals. Differentiating that sum with respect to each coefficient gives the normal equations X′ê=0. In ordinary notation, this means ΣᵢXᵢⱼêᵢ=0 for every regressor j. A zero sum of residuals follows only when the model contains an intercept, represented by a column of ones. This model has no intercept, so statement 1 and statement 3 are not always true. Also, Y=Xβ̂+ê, hence Y′ê=β̂′X′ê+ê′ê=ê′ê, not generally zero. Only statement 2 is always true. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation or regression is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: regression-t2 · effect of changing measurement units on OLS
items.stem: In a simple linear regression Yᵢ=α+βXᵢ+εᵢ, both X and Y are converted from square feet to square metres by multiplying every observation by the same conversion constant c. What happens to the fitted intercept and slope?
options: The intercept may change, but the slope will not change
The slope may change, but the intercept will not change
Both the intercept and slope may change
Neither the intercept nor the slope will change
items.explanation: Let Xᵢ*=cXᵢ and Yᵢ*=cYᵢ. The OLS slope is Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)(Yᵢ−Ȳ)/Σ(Xᵢ−X̄)². After conversion, the numerator and denominator are both multiplied by c², so their ratio β̂ is unchanged. The intercept is α̂=Ȳ−β̂X̄; after conversion it becomes cȲ−β̂(cX̄)=cα̂. So the intercept changes with the measurement scale, while the slope remains the same when both variables use the same conversion factor. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation or regression is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: regression-t2 · least-squares estimation, normal-theory MLE and BLUE
items.stem: Consider the model Yᵢ=α+βxᵢ+εᵢ, i=1,2,3, where xᵢ are fixed and the errors are independent N(0,σ²), with α, β and σ² unknown. The observations are (xᵢ,yᵢ)=(1,2.1),(2,3.9),(3,6). Which statements are true?
statements: The maximum-likelihood estimate of α is 0.1.
The least-squares estimate of α is 0.1.
The best linear unbiased estimate of α is 0.1.
The maximum-likelihood estimate of β/α is 19.5.

A.why: The fitted intercept is 0.1, so the MLE and least-squares estimate agree.

B.why: For this normal linear model, least squares minimises the residual sum of squares and gives the intercept 0.1.

C.why: Under the stated independent equal-variance error model, the least-squares estimator is BLUE by the Gauss–Markov theorem.

D.why: The estimated slope is 1.95 and the estimated intercept is 0.1, so their ratio is 19.5.

items.explanation: First calculate the sample means: x̄=(1+2+3)/3=2 and ȳ=(2.1+3.9+6)/3=4. The least-squares slope is β̂=Σ(xᵢ−x̄)(yᵢ−ȳ)/Σ(xᵢ−x̄)². The numerator is (−1)(−1.9)+0(−0.1)+1(2)=3.9, and the denominator is 1+0+1=2. Thus β̂=3.9/2=1.95. The intercept is α̂=ȳ−β̂x̄=4−1.95(2)=0.1. In a normal linear regression model, maximising the likelihood over α and β gives the same estimates as least squares, so statements 1 and 2 are true. Because the errors are independent with common variance, the Gauss–Markov theorem says the least-squares estimator is BLUE, so statement 3 is true. Finally β̂/α̂=1.95/0.1=19.5, so statement 4 is true. Therefore all four statements are correct. Other-exam relevance: normal linear regression, least squares, MLE and BLUE are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: regression-t2 · unbiasedness and variance comparison of through-origin and intercept OLS slopes
items.stem: Consider Yᵢ=βXᵢ+εᵢ, i=1,…,n, where εᵢ are i.i.d. N(0,σ²) and the nonrandom regressors Xᵢ are positive and distinct. Define β̂₁=∑(Yᵢ−Ȳ)(Xᵢ−X̄)/∑(Xᵢ−X̄)² and β̂₂=∑YᵢXᵢ/∑Xᵢ². Which statements are correct?
statements: Both β̂₁ and β̂₂ are unbiased estimators of β.
β̂₁ has larger variance than β̂₂.
β̂₂ has larger variance than β̂₁.
β̂₁ has the same variance as β̂₂.

A.why: Both estimators are linear in Y and have expectation β under the stated zero-mean error model. The variance of β̂₁ is σ²/∑(Xᵢ−X̄)², while the variance of β̂₂ is σ²/∑Xᵢ². Since ∑Xᵢ²=∑(Xᵢ−X̄)²+nX̄² and X̄>0, β̂₂ has the smaller variance.

B.why: This reverses the variance comparison; the through-origin estimator β̂₂ has the smaller variance here.

C.why: The variance ordering is the opposite.

D.why: The variances are not equal because nX̄²>0.

items.explanation: For β̂₁, substitute Yᵢ=βXᵢ+εᵢ. The deterministic part gives β and the error part has expectation zero, so E(β̂₁)=β. Similarly, β̂₂=β+∑Xᵢεᵢ/∑Xᵢ², so E(β̂₂)=β. Thus statement 1 is true. Since the errors are independent with variance σ², Var(β̂₁)=σ²/∑(Xᵢ−X̄)² and Var(β̂₂)=σ²/∑Xᵢ². Now ∑Xᵢ²=∑(Xᵢ−X̄)²+nX̄². Every Xᵢ is positive, so X̄>0 and the denominator for β̂₂ is strictly larger. Therefore Var(β̂₂)<Var(β̂₁), making statement 2 true. Statements 3 and 4 are false. Other-exam relevance: unbiased linear estimation and variance comparison in regression are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi; this is topic overlap, not a claim of an exact repeat.

items.topic: regression-t7 · heteroscedasticity and weighted least squares / BLUE
items.stem: Consider the simple linear regression model Yᵢ=βxᵢ+εᵢ, i=1,…,n, where E(εᵢ)=0, Cov(εᵢ,εₖ)=0 for i≠k, and Var(εᵢ)=xᵢ²σ². The xᵢ are fixed and nonzero. Which expression is the best linear unbiased estimator of β?
items.explanation: The error variance is not constant: Var(εᵢ)=xᵢ²σ². Divide the model by xᵢ: Yᵢ/xᵢ=β+εᵢ/xᵢ. The transformed errors εᵢ/xᵢ have mean zero, are uncorrelated, and each has variance Var(εᵢ/xᵢ)=xᵢ²σ²/xᵢ²=σ². Thus the transformed model has a common error variance and a constant mean β. The least-squares estimator of this common mean is the average of the transformed observations: β̂=(1/n)∑(Yᵢ/xᵢ). By the Gauss–Markov theorem applied to the transformed model, this is BLUE. Hence option 3 is correct. Other-exam relevance: weighted least squares, heteroscedasticity and BLUE are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi; this is topic overlap, not a claim of an exact repeat.
